action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. Before any measurement programme can function, every instrument requires a well-characterized baseline under controlled conditions. Starting with pendulum_lab: 12 trials will establish mean period, standard deviation, and drift signature. This is foundational work—no hypothesis testing possible until baselines exist. Pendulum chosen first as it is least sensitive to environmental coupling and most tolerant of setup variation; will use results to inform calibration strategy for resonator_lab before end of week.

Running 12 more trials (reaching n=30 by Day 2 end) will solidify the baseline, permit early drift detection, and increase precision of the mean estimate. This is methodologically prior to any cross-checks or hypothesis work. The instrument is accessible here at the lab and requires no special conditions.

High priority: an uncalibrated baseline is worse than no baseline.

Continuing systematic baseline accumulation on the primary instrument is the highest priority before the baseline window closes.

Day 10 audit identified time-alignment as the highest-priority systematic check. The pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_obs pairing shows the strongest cross-correlation (r=0.353 at 1-day offset, n=54), and both are co-located at the observatory. By taking 12 fresh side-by-side trials on pendulum_obs TODAY alongside resonator_obs (which I will also run), I can verify: (1) whether the 1-day offset is an artifact of asynchronous sampling or a real lagged coupling; (2) whether my time-alignment method is sound by checking same-day agreement; (3) whether within-stream reproducibility improves on a single day (ruling out short-term noise dominance). This directly tests my highest-prior hypothesis (0.35: environmental coupling masked by noise) and my concern about systematic method error (0.15). If same-day pendulum_obs and resonator_obs readings show weak correlation, the 1-day offset is likely a sampling artifact and I need to re-examine my offset calculation. If they show strong correlation at zero offset, I have found the smoking gun for shared environmental sensitivity and can begin environmental monitoring. Either way, this measurement will constrain the most suspicious pattern in my data.

Day 11 showed pendulum_obs post-baseline mean 2.5097 (n=18), a +1.51σ drift from baseline 2.4996. This is the largest single-instrument drift signal in my notebook and the only measurement stream showing a consistent upward trend post-Day 10. Before I can trust the Day 10 correlation analysis or audit time-alignment issues, I must rule out instrumental drift on pendulum_obs itself. The observatory pendulum is also my best co-located pair (with resonator_obs, r=0.316 at 6-day offset). Twelve fresh trials today will (1) test whether the Day 11 elevation persists or was sampling noise, (2) give me current baseline-to-now comparison with high n, and (3) provide the tightest same-day pair with resonator_obs to test the 1-day offset hypothesis directly. If pendulum_obs is genuinely drifting, I need to know before I invest effort in cross-instrument forensics.

This is a direct, low-cost test of my highest-probability hypothesis (0.35: environmental coupling with time lag) and addresses the systematic-error concern (0.15: are the offsets real or artifacts of my method?) by checking reproducibility.

If the 6-day offset persists after this audit, I will elevate 'real environmental coupling' to p ≥ 0.40. If it vanishes, I will drop systematic error to p ≤ 0.05 and focus on measurement noise and sparse sampling as the dominant sources of weak correlation. This is methodologically sound: I must rule out my own error before claiming a puzzle in nature.

DATA PIPELINE AUDIT: Before I can trust any hypothesis about physics, I must eliminate the possibility that my timestamping or trial-to-date alignment is systematically wrong. The repeated 6-day offset in cross-correlations (pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_lab, pendulum_lab ↔ pendulum_obs) is too convenient and suggests a mapping error.
